items.title: An upper sum for a cube
items.prose: Take $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 1]$ with two equal pieces, $[0, \tfrac12]$ and $[\tfrac12, 1]$.
items.question: What is the upper sum $U$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $x^3$ rises, so use the right ends $\tfrac12$ and 1, times the width $\tfrac12$.

byKey.left: You used the left ends, which give the lower sum $\tfrac{1}{16}$ for a rising $f$.
byKey.no-width: You added the tops, $\tfrac98$, but did not multiply by the width $\tfrac12$.

explain.text: $x^3$ rises, so each top is at the right end: $\tfrac18$ and 1. So $U = \tfrac12 \times \tfrac98 = \tfrac{9}{16} = 0.5625$, and $L = \tfrac{1}{16}$. The integral $\tfrac14$ lies between.

items.title: A function that is x on the rationals
items.prose: Let $f(x) = x$ for rational $x$ and $f(x) = 0$ for irrational $x$, on $[0, 1]$.
items.question: Is $f$ integrable?

options.text: No: $L(f, P) = 0$ for every $P$, while every $U(f, P)$ is at least $\tfrac12$.
Yes, with integral 0, since rationals are rare.
options.why: Upper sums see every rational. On each piece the sup is the right end, so $U(f, P) = U(x, P) \ge \tfrac12$.

options.text: Yes, with integral $\tfrac14$, half of $\int_0^1 x\,dx$.
options.why: You averaged the two rules. The sums use sup and inf, which stay $\ge \tfrac12$ and 0.
Continuity at one point is not enough. $f$ is discontinuous at every $x > 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sup and inf of $f$ on a piece $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$.

explain.text: By density, each piece has $\sup f = x_k$ and $\inf f = 0$. So $U(f, P) = U(x, P) \ge \int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac12$ and $L(f, P) = 0$. The gap never closes.

items.title: A derivative with a cubed limit
items.question: What is $F'(x)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use part one at the upper limit $x^3$, times the chain-rule factor $3x^2$.

byKey.nochain: You forgot the chain rule. The limit $x^3$ moves at rate $3x^2$.
byKey.lnx: You read $\ln t$ at $x$. It is read at the upper limit, $t = x^3$.

explain.text: With $H(u) = \int_1^u \ln t\,dt$, part one gives $H'(u) = \ln u$, since $\ln$ is continuous. So $F'(x) = H'(x^3) \cdot 3x^2 = 3x^2\ln(x^3) = 9x^2\ln x$.

items.title: Area so far under a step
items.question: What is $F(2.5)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the signed area over $[0, 1]$ and over $[1, 2.5]$.

byKey.abs: You added the areas as if both were positive. Below the axis counts negative.
byKey.value: You gave $f(2.5)$. $F$ is the area so far.

explain.text: $\int_0^1 2 = 2$ and $\int_1^{2.5} (-1) = -1.5$, so $F(2.5) = 0.5$. $F$ rises with slope 2, then falls with slope 1. It has a corner at 1, where $f$ jumps.

items.title: Which axiom fails
items.prose: Let $d(x, y) = (x - y)^2 + |x - y|$ on $\mathbb{R}$. At the points 0, 1, 2: $d(0, 2) = 6$, while $d(0, 1) + d(1, 2) = 2 + 2 = 4$.
items.question: Which metric axiom fails?

options.why: Both terms are unchanged when $x$ and $y$ swap.

options.text: None: adding a metric to a non-negative term gives a metric.
options.why: The added $(x - y)^2$ breaks the triangle inequality, as $6 > 4$ shows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $d(0, 2)$ with $d(0, 1) + d(1, 2)$.

explain.text: $d(0, 2) = 4 + 2 = 6$ but $d(0, 1) + d(1, 2) = 4$. The squared term makes long steps cost more than two short ones. The other two axioms hold.

items.title: Room in the unit disc
items.prose: In the plane with the straight-line metric, take the open unit disc $B(0, 1)$ and the point $p = (0.3, 0.4)$.
items.question: What is the largest $r$ with $B(p, r) \subseteq B(0, 1)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $p$'s distance from 0 from the radius 1.

byKey.coord: You used $1 - 0.4$, the room up to the square's edge. The disc's edge is nearer, along the ray from 0.
byKey.dist: You stopped at $0.3^2 + 0.4^2 = 0.25$. Take the root, 0.5, and subtract from 1.

explain.text: $d(0, p) = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, so $r = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5$. If $d(p, y) < 0.5$, then $d(0, y) < 0.5 + 0.5 = 1$. No larger ball fits, along the ray through $p$.

items.title: A set with its limit added
items.question: Is $A$ closed?

options.text: Yes: a convergent sequence in $A$ tends to 1 or is eventually constant, and both limits lie in $A$.
No: a set of separate points is never closed.
options.why: Finite sets of points are closed, and so is this one, since it keeps its only limit point 1.

options.text: No: it is not open, so it is not closed.
options.why: Not open does not mean closed, nor the reverse. Test closedness by limits.
Closed sets need not be intervals: $\{0\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ are closed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the limits of convergent sequences in $A$ and check they are in $A$.

explain.text: The only point that terms of $A$ crowd towards is 1, and $1 \in A$. Any other convergent sequence in $A$ is eventually constant. So $A$ contains all its limits and is closed; without 1 it would not be.

items.title: A closed interval with a hole
items.prose: Let $K = [0, 1] \setminus \{\tfrac12\}$, the closed unit interval with its midpoint removed.
items.question: Is $K$ compact?

options.text: No: $x_n = \tfrac12 - \tfrac1{n+2}$ lies in $K$ and every subsequence tends to $\tfrac12 \notin K$.
Yes: it is bounded and lies inside the compact $[0, 1]$.
options.why: A subset of a compact set is compact only if it is closed. $K$ is not closed.

options.text: Yes: it contains both end points 0 and 1.
options.why: Containing the ends is not enough. The hole at $\tfrac12$ lets a limit escape.
$K \subseteq [0, 1]$ is bounded. It fails closedness instead.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a sequence in $K$ whose limit is the missing point.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 - \tfrac1{n+2}$ is in $K$ and tends to $\tfrac12$, so every subsequence does too. The limit is not in $K$, so $K$ is not compact. By Heine-Borel it fails because it is not closed.

items.title: A uniform delta for the square root
items.prose: $\sqrt x$ is continuous on the compact $[0, 1]$, so it is uniformly continuous. Indeed $|\sqrt x - \sqrt y| \le \sqrt{|x - y|}$ for $x, y \ge 0$.
items.question: Which $\delta$ does this bound give for $\varepsilon = 0.1$?

feedback.correct: Right. $\delta = \varepsilon^2 = 0.01$, the same at every point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\sqrt{|x - y|} < 0.1$ for $|x - y|$.

explain.text: $|x - y| < 0.01$ gives $|\sqrt x - \sqrt y| \le \sqrt{|x - y|} < 0.1$. So $\delta = \varepsilon^2 = 0.01$ works everywhere on $[0, 1]$. Near 0 the slope of $\sqrt x$ is unbounded, yet one $\delta$ still serves.
